inline.s: The ālaya too is just like this: both being and non-being it flees.
When consciousness turns and takes new reliance, the mind is free from turbid confusion;
This mind I call the Buddha, for it awakens to every dharma.
Forever cut are the three continuities, and the four propositions left aside;
Both being and non-being are cast away, for all existences are forever like illusion.
The first seven stages arise from the mind, and so a twofold nature springs;
Upon the remaining stages, and the Buddha's, perfect truth is seen.
The realms of desire, of form, and of no-form, and also nirvāṇa—
all the bodies there are the mind's own domain.
Whenever something is gained, just then does confusion arise;
but when one has awakened to one's own mind, confusion does not arise.
I establish two kinds of dharma: the marks, and the realization;
by four modes of reasoning, as means, I set forth the accomplishment.
To see the various names and marks is deluded discrimination;
when one is free of names and marks, one dwells in the stainless nature.
Following the discrimination of grasper and grasped, the imagined mark appears;
when one is free of that discrimination, one dwells in the nature's own.
When the mind is liberated, it is everlasting and true;
the buddha-nature and the dharma-nature, and suchness, hold no discrimination.
Because there is a mind that is pure, defilement is seen to appear;
with no purity there is no defilement: true purity is what the noble ones tread.
The world arises from conditions, and grows through discrimination;
beholding it as illusion and dream, one is at that moment freed.
The manifold evil habitual tendencies are commingled with the mind;
and so beings see an outer realm, and never behold the mind's own nature.
The mind's nature is intrinsically pure, and gives rise to no confusions;
confusion rises from evil habit—and therefore one does not see the mind.
Confusion itself is the real; the real is nowhere else;
for the formations are no formations, and are seen nowhere else.
If one beholds all that is conditioned, far from the grasped and the grasper,
then, by being free of every mark, one sees the world as mind alone.
Abiding securely in mind-only, one discriminates no outer realm;
one dwells upon the object that is suchness, and passes beyond the mind's own measure.
When one has passed beyond the mind's own measure, one passes beyond the markless too;
for one who dwells in the markless cannot see the Great Vehicle.
With action stilled and effort spent, one purifies the great vows;
and because it is markless, my own supreme wisdom is not seen.
One should behold what the mind ranges over, and behold what wisdom ranges over;
beholding what insight ranges over, one is not confused about marks.
What the mind ranges over is the truth of suffering; what wisdom ranges over is its origin;
the remaining two truths, and the Buddha-stage, are all what insight ranges over.
The winning of the fruit and of nirvāṇa, and the noble eightfold path,
and the awakening to every dharma—this is the Buddha's stainless wisdom.
The eye as faculty, the field of form, space, light, and the turning of attention—
by these, from out the ālaya, beings' eye-consciousness is born.
The grasper with the grasped and grasping, name and thing—all are nothing at all;
and to discriminate without a cause—this is what the unwise do.
Name and meaning do not give birth to one another, and name and meaning are not separate either;
to reckon that things arise from a cause, or from no cause, is never free of discrimination.
The fool says he abides in the ultimate truth, and speaks as his views decree;
but a single nature with five, thus it cannot be—so let the truth's meaning go.
Those who prattle of being and non-being—one should pass beyond such demons;
for having seen there is no self, one no longer craves existences.
Those who reckon the maker to be permanent, with spells and wrangling ways;
the ultimate truth is beyond all speech, and in it one beholds the quiescent dharma.
Relying upon the ālaya, therefore, the manas comes to turn;
and because mind and manas are its reliance, the various consciousnesses are born.
The dharmas that false imagining posits, and the mind's own nature of suchness—
thus does the man of samādhi contemplate, and comprehends the nature that is mind-only.
He contemplates the manas with the marks and their affairs, and thinks not of permanent or impermanent;
nor of arisen or unarisen—he discriminates neither of the two.
From out the ālaya there arise the various consciousnesses;
yet never upon a single meaning do two kinds of mind arise.
Because he sees his own mind, it is neither empty nor speakable;
but if one does not see one's own mind, one is bound in the net of views.
The conditions have no arising; the faculties have no existence;
there is no greed, no aggregate or element—nothing conditioned at all.
Deeds and their rewards were never there; there is no making, nothing made;
attachment was never there to begin with, so there is no bondage and no more.
There is no neutral dharma either, and neither dharma nor non-dharma;
there is no time, no nirvāṇa—the dharma-nature cannot be grasped.
It is not Buddha, not the ultimate truth, not a cause and not a fruit;
not an inversion, not nirvāṇa, not arising and not passing away.
Nor are there the twelve links, nor the extremes and the non-extremes;
every view is wholly cut away—and this I call mind-only.
Affliction, karma, and the body, and the fruit that karma yields;
all are like a flame, like a dream, like a city of the gandharvas.
Because one dwells in mind-only, all the marks are left behind;
because one dwells in mind-only, one can see both severance and permanence.
In nirvāṇa there are no aggregates, no self, and no mark;
by entering into mind-only, one wins liberation through the turning.
Because evil habit is the cause, the great earth appears as outer;
and so too all living beings—yet in mind-only nothing is seen.
Body, wealth, and land are images shown forth by beings' habits;
the mind is neither being nor non-being, but habit-energy keeps it hidden.
Stain appears within the pure, not purity within the stain;
as clouds obscure the open sky, so the mind does not appear.
The imagined nature one takes as existing, yet in dependent arising it is not;
through the deluded clinging of the imagined, dependent arising holds no discrimination.
Not everything made is form, and there is form that is not made;
dream-form, mirage-form, flame-form: these are not made at all.
If, regarding dharmas born of conditions, one calls them real or unreal,
such a one will surely rest upon the views of oneness and of difference.
Hearers are of three kinds: those born of aspiration and of transformation,
and those whose greed and hatred are gone—the ones born of the dharma.
Bodhisattvas too are of three kinds, not yet having a Buddha's marks;
thinking upon living beings, they manifest the Buddha's form.
Whatever is manifested by beings' minds arises all from habitual tendencies;
the manifold various images, like stars and clouds, the sun and moon.
If the great elements truly existed, then something made could arise from them;
but since the great elements have no nature, there is no grasper and no grasped.
The great elements are the maker, and earth and the rest are what is made;
but the great elements were never born, and so no made form exists.
The imagined and the real, and every form, and forms the illusion makes—
dream-form, mirage-form, and flame-form, which is the fifth.
The icchantikas are five in kind, and the lineages as well;
five vehicles and no vehicle, and nirvāṇa of six kinds.
The aggregates are twenty-four, and forms are of eight kinds;
the Buddhas are twenty-four, and the Buddha-sons are of two.
The dharma-gates are a hundred and eight, and the hearers are of three;
the Buddhalands are but one alone, and the Buddha likewise one.
Liberation is of three kinds, and the mind's outflows are four;
selflessness is of six kinds, and the knowables also four.
Far removed from any maker, and from every kind of view;
inner self-realization, unmoved—this is the supreme Great Vehicle.
The born and the unborn: of these there are eight kinds and nine;
in a single instant or by stages, the realized goal is one.
The formless realm has eight kinds, and the dhyānas differ sixfold,
the solitary buddhas and the Buddha-sons: deliverance is sevenfold.
In the three times nothing at all exists, nor permanent and impermanent;
